meta.titre: Relative Clauses: choosing the pronoun and the punctuation

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A mother in Bamenda tells her daughter, "The teacher who gave you the book wants to see me." Without the clause *who gave you the book*, the daughter would not know which teacher is meant. Relative clauses carry this kind of identifying detail in every text you read and write, and they recur in the grammar section of Paper 1, where you must choose the right word or name the type of clause. They are also what lets a good summary join two short sentences into one precise sentence.

items: A clause has its own subject and verb, and a relative clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.
An adjective describes a noun, and the noun described is called the antecedent when a pronoun refers back to it.
A preposition (*in*, *with*, *to*, *of*) is followed by a noun or a pronoun in the object form.

sections.titre: Relative pronouns, defining and non-defining clauses
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a relative clause does

A relative clause gives more information about a noun and comes straight after that noun. It begins with a relative pronoun (*who, whom, which, that, whose*) or a relative adverb (*where, when, why*). Because it does the work of an adjective, it is also called an **adjectival clause**. Do not confuse it with a noun clause (*I know what you mean*) or an adverbial clause (*He left because it was late*), which answer different questions.

| Word | Used for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| who | people | The nurse who helped us was kind. |
| whom | people, as the object | The man whom we met was a lawyer. |
| which | things and animals | The bag which I bought is blue. |
| that | people or things, defining clauses only | The book that I borrowed is old. |
| whose | possession | The boy whose bag was lost cried. |
| where | places | The village where he grew up is small. |
| when | times | I remember the day when we met. |
| why | reasons | Tell me the reason why you left. |

### Defining and non-defining clauses

A **defining** clause identifies the noun: without it the sentence is incomplete. It has no commas, it may use *that*, and an object pronoun can be dropped: *The book (that) I borrowed is old.*

A **non-defining** clause only adds extra information and is separated by commas. It never uses *that*, and the pronoun can never be dropped: *Mrs Fonge, who teaches us history, is retiring.* Compare *My sister who lives in Buea is a nurse* (it suggests that I have other sisters) with *My sister, who lives in Buea, is a nurse* (the clause is extra information).

### The relative word must match its role

Choose the word by asking two questions. Is the antecedent a person, a thing or a place? What is the word doing inside its own clause: subject, object, possessor or object of a preposition? The relative word already stands for the noun, so the pronoun is never repeated: *the phone which I bought* (not *which I bought it*).

### Preposition and relative pronoun

In formal English the preposition comes before *whom* or *which*: *the teacher to whom I wrote*, *the house in which we live*. After a preposition we cannot use *who* or *that*. In informal English the preposition moves to the end: *the teacher I wrote to*.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the antecedent is a place, a time or a reason
variantes.contenu_markdown: *Where* can replace *in which*, *at which* or *to which* after a place: *the town where we spent our holiday* means *the town in which we spent our holiday*. After *time* and *day*, use *when* or *on which*. After *reason*, use *why* or *that*: *the reason why he left*. The adverb is not followed by a second preposition: write *the room where we met*, not *the room where we met in*.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the clause says that the antecedent owns something
variantes.contenu_markdown: *Whose* replaces *his, her, its* or *their* and is followed by a noun: *The girl whose bag was stolen reported it.* It can refer to things as well (*a house whose roof is damaged*), and it is not the same word as *who's*, which means *who is* or *who has*.

variantes.nom: Which for a whole idea; that after strong words
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the clause comments on a whole sentence, or the antecedent is all, everything, nothing, the only or a superlative
variantes.contenu_markdown: A non-defining *which* can refer to the whole of the earlier clause: *He passed the exam, which surprised everyone.* After *all, everything, nothing, the only* and a superlative, standard English prefers *that* (or no pronoun): *Everything that she said was true. The best film that I have seen.*

sections.enonce_markdown:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.

Mr Ndi, ______ car broke down on the way, arrived late for the meeting.

A) who   B) whom   C) whose   D) which

etapes.justification: The commas around the clause show that it adds extra information about a named person, so the clause is non-defining.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Non-defining clause about Mr Ndi (a person).

etapes.action: Find the relation between the antecedent and the next noun.
etapes.justification: The word that follows the gap is *car*, and the car belongs to Mr Ndi.
Split the clause: *Mr Ndi's car broke down on the way.* This confirms that the missing word replaces *Mr Ndi's*.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The missing word replaces a possessive.

etapes.justification: *Who* and *whom* would need a verb or a subject next, not the noun *car*. *Which* refers to things, not to a person.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A, B and D cannot be followed by *car* in this meaning.

etapes.justification: The completed sentence must be grammatical and keep the commas.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *Mr Ndi, whose car broke down on the way, arrived late for the meeting.*

sections.conclusion_markdown: The answer is **C) whose**. The clause is a non-defining relative clause, and *whose* expresses that the car belongs to Mr Ndi.

items.erreur_markdown: *The woman which sold me the cloth was friendly.*
items.pourquoi_faux: *Which* is used for things and animals. The antecedent is a person.
items.correction_markdown: *The woman who sold me the cloth was friendly.* (*That* is also possible in a defining clause.)

items.erreur_markdown: *My uncle, that lives in Buea, is a mechanic.*
items.pourquoi_faux: *That* is not used in a non-defining clause, that is, a clause between commas.
items.correction_markdown: *My uncle, who lives in Buea, is a mechanic.*

items.erreur_markdown: *The phone which I bought it last week has stopped working.*
items.pourquoi_faux: The relative pronoun already stands for the noun. Repeating the noun as *it* gives the object twice.
items.correction_markdown: *The phone which I bought last week has stopped working.*

items.erreur_markdown: *The boy who's bag was stolen reported it to the police.*
items.pourquoi_faux: *Who's* means *who is* or *who has*. Possession is expressed by *whose*.
items.correction_markdown: *The boy whose bag was stolen reported it to the police.*

items.erreur_markdown: *The friend with who I travelled is a teacher.*
items.pourquoi_faux: After a preposition, formal English requires *whom*, not *who*.
items.correction_markdown: *The friend with whom I travelled is a teacher.*

items.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct word.

The farmer ______ sells yams at the roadside is my uncle.

A) which   B) whom   C) whose   D) who
items.solution_markdown: The antecedent *the farmer* is a person and is the subject of *sells*. *Who* is the subject form for people. Answer: **D) who**. *Which* is for things, *whom* is an object form, and *whose* would need a noun after it.

items.enonce_markdown:
Join each pair of sentences with a relative clause.

(a) The town is quiet. We spent our holiday there.
(b) Mrs Tabi teaches us French. She comes from Limbe.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) *The town where we spent our holiday is quiet.* (or *The town in which we spent our holiday is quiet.*) It is a defining clause, so there are no commas.

(b) *Mrs Tabi, who teaches us French, comes from Limbe.* (or *Mrs Tabi, who comes from Limbe, teaches us French.*) The name already identifies her, so the clause is non-defining and needs commas, and *that* cannot be used.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Name the type of the clause in bold: *My brother, **who studies in Yaounde**, is coming home.*

(b) Correct the sentence: *The pupils whom I taught them last year have all passed.*

(c) Choose the correct word: *Everything ______ she told us was true.* A) what   B) that   C) whom   D) where

(d) Rewrite with the preposition before the relative pronoun: *The man I was speaking to is the new principal.*
items.solution_markdown:
(a) It is a **non-defining relative clause** (an adjectival clause), because it adds extra information about *my brother* and is set off by commas.

(b) The relative pronoun *whom* already stands for the pupils, so the object pronoun *them* must go: **The pupils whom I taught last year have all passed.**

(c) After *everything*, standard English uses *that*: **B) that**. *What* cannot follow *everything*, *whom* is for people, and *where* is for places.

(d) The preposition *to* goes before *whom*: **The man to whom I was speaking is the new principal.**

items_markdown: A relative clause is an adjectival clause: it follows a noun and begins with who, whom, which, that, whose, where, when or why.
Use *who* for people, *which* for things and animals, *whose* for possession, and *where* for places.
A defining clause identifies the noun and has no commas; a non-defining clause adds extra information, takes commas, and never uses *that*.
Never repeat the noun after the relative pronoun, and do not confuse *whose* with *who's*.
After a preposition use *whom* or *which*, never *who* or *that*: *with whom*, *in which*.
